title: Let's Talk About Homework
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino argues that homework is treated as an assumed part of teaching practice without the training or evidence base given to other areas like questioning or feedback, and that research on homework's effectiveness is too methodologically inconsistent to settle the debate either way. Rather than relitigating whether homework works, she reframes the question around what makes homework effective: teachers need the same principle applied in lessons, teach something, then provide spaced opportunities to practise and rehearse it, applied to independent study skills too. She lays out a framework of stakeholder questions covering the teacher's view (does the homework have value, is it sustainable to set and give feedback on), the student's view (do they have a suitable space, do they feel motivated, do they understand its purpose), the parent's view (do they understand why it's set and how to support it), and the school's culture (is effort recognised, is homework explicitly linked to classroom learning). She presents this multi-stakeholder framework as the foundation of her book The Homework Conundrum, and closes by arguing that homework deserves the same serious, ongoing conversation in CPD that other areas of teaching already receive.
points: Castelino argues homework is uniquely under-trained among teaching practices: teachers receive extensive CPD on questioning and feedback but rarely any on what makes homework effective.
She reframes homework through the same instructional principle used in lessons, teach, then provide spaced practice and rehearsal, applied specifically to independent study skills.
Her four-stakeholder framework (teacher, student, parent, school culture) breaks 'does homework work' into a longer list of conditional questions about value, sustainability, and motivation.
She positions the whole framework as the basis of her book The Homework Conundrum, aimed at helping schools build a positive, sustainable homework culture.
quotes: When I was a child, I hated it. It was too much, the consequences of not doing it were severe, my teachers never really acknowledged my effort or thinking.
No one spoke about homework and yet I was expected to set it. I never had any training on it or what features affected its effectiveness.
The trouble with the research on homework, however, is the variability in methodology, ages of participants and types of homework.

In our lessons, we teach something new and then provide opportinities for our students to practise and rehearse, coming back to it and building on it over time. This same principle applies to independent study skills.

But there are many factors to consider when setting effective homework. When we consider these factors together, we have a greater chance at setting homework that can positively influence student learning.
It is my hope that conversations about learning include homework, so it is truly a part of classroom learning.
